extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of early-18th-century English periodicals, literary historians, and theatre historians
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated edition of early-18th-century periodical essays (Tatler/Spectator style) with editorial notes and historical commentary on social manners, theatre, and morals. The page contains original prose plus footnotes explaining persons, plays, and historical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman (man of conversation) — essential qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Warmth of imagination, quick relish of pleasure, and a manner of becoming it; the height of good breeding is shown rather in never giving offence than in doing obliging things; the most necessary talent is a good judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded guidance: a good judgment enables a man to be master of his companion without letting him see it, to act with ease among men of pleasure and with despatch among men of business, to refuse engagements in a manner that convinces the asker they ought not to have asked, to maintain equality of society so each obliges as much as is obliged, to combine cheerful spirit with discretion (not appear cunning), and to be as just and discreet as if there were no law or calumny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretty Fellow (artificial mimicry) — anti-pattern for manners
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Pretty Fellow' attains reputation by artificial behaviour imitating a naturally agreeable man; he is a perfect mimic of the elegant companion but in reality the most unlike him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs and examples: preening before the mirror, meditating to contrive an air, returning to the glass to recollect 'forgetfulness.' Presented as a negative standard — affectation and artifice rather than genuine judgment and ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of costume over dialect for character identification in plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern writers rely on hats, swords, wigs, shoes and dress to show a man's character (counsellor, fop, courtier, or citizen) rather than forcing different dialects or speech for each character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: this method makes the writing and representation easier and more accessible to audiences; caveat: it may reduce the need for verbal distinction among characters and can simplify character construction at the cost of depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness of character voices (ideal of dramatic writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No one sentence in a play should be spoken by any one character, which could possibly enter into the head of any other man represented in it; but every sentiment should be peculiar to him only."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion: Ben Jonson's plays are praised for maintaining separate passions and discourses for characters; practical note/anti-pattern: enforcing absolute distinctiveness may render most modern plays too short, and present writers often cannot or should not be examined to that extreme standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: humour supported by action as a criterion of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor's action and physical performance can supply humour where the text lacks a distinct 'humour' — example: Mr. Estcourt's action in Sergeant Kite admirably supplies the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation note: judge actors not only by line delivery but by their physical action and observation; action can compensate for weaknesses in the written humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre profession's social purpose and moderation of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors as tradesmen who, after their day's work, perform for modest wages; theatre profits should serve public goods (e.g., maintaining a hospital) rather than allowing actors to grow rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amsterdam actors are journeymen earning a guilder a night; profits maintain a hospital. Comparative note: English playhouses have similar charitable outcomes (e.g., Dulwich Hospital founded by an actor). This frames theatre as a civic profession rather than purely lucrative entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful ogling/gaze as courtship technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful courtship requires 'an exquisite judgment' to read and time the language of her eyes and 'not let yours talk too fast for hers' — the watchful glance and waiting for the 'second twinkle' are decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: ogling is an art that few possess; it involves measured attention, reciprocal signals, and the cultivation of pleasing inner images that transform perception. Presented as prescriptive social advice for men of fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations and social costs before pursuing public divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Before bringing a private marital grievance into open court, one must consider the mortifications of public trial, impertinent whispers of the people present, licentious reflections of the pleaders, and public interpretations of one's conduct; curbing desires is a virtue and public suits invite scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: the law may redress the grievance, but the social cost (public scandal, loss of reputation) may outweigh legal remedy; alternatives and admonitions (e.g., private abstinence, seclusion) are discussed rather than immediate litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical social enforcement (naming of fantastical dress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly marking and shaming those who appear in fantastical habit contrary to present fashion by inserting their name and dress in the next publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a normative enforcement mechanism within the periodical's social commentary — an explicit sanction (public naming) to enforce conformity to fashion norms; given as a jocular public notice rather than a formal rule.
